subjects.introduction: To be in the water and not get wet: so ‘Abdu’l-Bahá is reported to have described the life Bahá’u’lláh asks of us, fully at work in the world yet unpossessed by it. Detachment is not the absence of means but the freedom of the heart; a person may trade, build, wear silk and prosper, so long as nothing stands between the soul and its Maker. Gleanings section CXXVIII defines the world itself as unawareness of one’s Maker [1], which makes renunciation less a flight from life than a way of seeing it clearly. The way leads inward, to the surrender of self and will, and to the seeker who must empty the heart of love and hate before truth can be found. Its highest fruit is patience: the Ishráqát closes with a counsel to be patient [2], a letter written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi extends that patience to oneself [3], and the Qur’án [4] and the Dhammapada [5] speak of persevering and of conquering the self. From here the path continues toward contentment, toward tests and trials, and toward trust in God.

Detachment here turns inward to self, will and motive. The Hidden Words and other Tablets speak of renouncing self and coming forth from the sheath of self and desire, and the Báb counsels worship free of fear of the fire or hope of paradise. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá qualifies the language of self-forgetfulness: it means overcoming blameworthy promptings and does not mean letting one’s physical health deteriorate. A reported talk adds that renunciation does not suppress noble feelings or shift responsibility. Other passages name three things to renounce and three to attain, and find true bravery in conquering one’s own self. How does losing the self differ from neglecting it? Which passage best shows how surrender of will can coexist with responsibility?

order.why: The Kitáb-i-Íqán, the Seven Valleys, the Gems of Divine Mysteries and related texts make detachment a condition of understanding. Read these as conditions of inquiry rather than as a dismissal of learning. What does impartiality require of a seeker? Which attachments most often obstruct understanding?
shortened: No man shall attain the shores of the ocean of true understanding except he be detached from all that is in heaven and on earth.

He must never seek to exalt himself above anyone, must wash away from the tablet of his heart every trace of pride and vainglory, must cling unto patience and resignation, observe silence, and refrain from idle talk.

Patience is presented as the companion and the fruit of detachment. One Tablet calls patience the highest fruit of the tree of detachment; another tells of a garden in the precincts of eternity named Patience; a third recalls that every good deed has its measure of reward except patience. The readings set patience within tribulation, separation, waiting and loss, and the Báb writes that He awaits the decree as sweeter than honey. Other passages join patience with gratitude, with gracious concealment of others’ faults, and with refusal to retaliate. How does patience differ from passivity or resignation to wrongdoing? What does patience ask of a person toward others?
shortened: Know ye that trials and tribulations have, from time immemorial, been the lot of the chosen Ones of God and His beloved, and such of His servants as are detached from all else but Him, they whom neither merchandise nor traffic beguile from the remembrance of the Almighty, they that speak not till He hath spoken, and act according to His commandment. Such is God's method carried into effect of old, and such will it remain in the future. Blessed are the steadfastly enduring, they that are patient under ills and hardships, who lament not over anything that befalleth them, and who tread the path of resignation.

One Tablet calls patience the highest fruit of the tree of detachment; another tells of a garden in the precincts of eternity named Patience; a third recalls that every good deed has its measure of reward except patience. The readings set patience within tribulation, separation, waiting and loss, and the Báb writes that He awaits the decree as sweeter than honey. Other passages join patience with gratitude, with gracious concealment of others’ faults, and with refusal to retaliate. How does patience differ from passivity or resignation to wrongdoing? What does patience ask of a person toward others?
